nameStory: This tiny sea snail's scientific name Frigidoalvania brychia tells us it's adapted to cold waters - 'frigid' refers to the chilly North Atlantic where it makes its home. The name brychia comes from Greek, though the exact meaning remains a mystery to most shell collectors, adding to this little mollusk's intrigue.
description: Frigidoalvania brychia is an incredibly tiny sea snail, so small it's classified as a micromollusk - you'd need a magnifying glass to see its details clearly. Like other spire-shells in the Rissoidae family, it has a tall, pointed spiral shell that looks like a miniature ice cream cone. These marine gastropods are true ocean dwellers, spending their entire lives in saltwater environments. Despite their microscopic size, they're complete snails with all the features of their larger cousins.

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Extremely small shell, typically requiring magnification to see clearly - much smaller than your pinky nail

idTips.label: Spire shape
idTips.description: Tall, pointed shell that spirals upward like a tiny cone or church steeple

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: Smooth, glossy surface that may appear almost glassy when viewed under magnification

idTips.label: Marine habitat only
idTips.description: Found exclusively in saltwater environments - never in freshwater ponds or streams

habitat: This marine micromollusk lives in the cold waters off New England's rocky coastline, particularly in deeper offshore areas. You're most likely to encounter empty shells washed up on beaches after storms, mixed in with other tiny shells and sea debris. Look for them along rocky shores and beaches from Maine to Massachusetts, especially after strong onshore winds bring deep-water materials to shore.

seasonality.spring: Storm-tossed shells may wash ashore during spring storms. Living specimens are active in offshore waters as temperatures begin to rise.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for finding empty shells on beaches during calm weather beach-combing. Living animals are most active in cooler deeper waters.
seasonality.fall: Autumn storms frequently bring shells to shore. This may be the best season for finding specimens mixed with other marine debris.
seasonality.winter: Harsh winter storms can deposit shells on beaches, though cold conditions make beach searching less pleasant. Living animals remain active in deep, cold waters.

funFact: Despite being so incredibly tiny that dozens could fit on your thumbnail, this little snail is a complete predator with a ribbon-like feeding structure called a radula that works like a tiny cheese grater to scrape food from surfaces underwater.
confusionNotes: Can be confused with other microscopic marine snails, but its exclusively marine habitat separates it from any freshwater micromollusks. The tall spire shape distinguishes it from rounder micromollusks, though you'll need magnification to see these details clearly.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'micromollusk' refers to any mollusk smaller than 5-10mm - these tiny creatures are often overlooked but represent a huge portion of marine biodiversity. Many beachcombers walk right past thousands of these microscopic shells without realizing they're there.
compareHints: Since this is the only Frigidoalvania species recorded in New England waters, compare it to other members of the spire-shell family (Rissoidae) by its extremely small size and preference for colder, deeper waters. Unlike some coastal relatives that live in tide pools, this species prefers the deeper, consistently cold offshore environment.
